Context/Background: In a prospective endometrial carcinoma (EC) cohort, we performed a differential analysis of protein levels between hotspot-mutated CTNNB1 and WT CTNNB1 tumors, in the CNV-L subgroup.  In a separate analysis, we found that CTNNB1 S45 phosphorylation was significantly downregulated in hotspot-mutated tumors, whereas phosphosites distant from the hotspot mutations were mostly upregulated.
Prompt: Provide a discussion of the results from the differential analysis and any relevance to the mutation state of CTNNB1.

Introduction/Context  
In a prospective endometrial carcinoma (EC) cohort restricted to the CNV-Low (CNV-L) molecular subgroup, protein abundance was compared between tumors harboring hotspot mutations in CTNNB1 versus wild-type CTNNB1.  The differential proteomic analysis (NIHMS1921121-supplement-7) identified 10 150 quantified proteins.  Among these, CTNNB1 itself was significantly upregulated in hotspot-mutant tumors (L2FC = 0.76, FDR = 1.7 × 10⁻¹¹), as was the negative Wnt regulator AXIN1 (L2FC = 0.67, FDR = 1.9 × 10⁻¹²).  Other key Wnt pathway effectors (e.g., LEF1, DKK4, APCDD1) also showed strong upregulation (L2FC > 1, FDR < 10⁻⁶).  Parallel phosphoproteomic profiling (not shown) demonstrated downregulation of CTNNB1 S45 phosphorylation in hotspot-mutant tumors, whereas distal CTNNB1 phosphosites were generally increased.  Details not specified for sample size or replicates.  

Keywords  
• CTNNB1 mutation • Wnt signaling • protein processing • ribosome/translation • cilium assembly  

Candidate Genes  
CTNNB1, AXIN1, LEF1, DKK4, APCDD1  

Pathway Enrichments

Analysis  
CTNNB1 hotspot mutations in CNV-L EC are associated with a broad proteomic shift: upregulation of core Wnt pathway components (CTNNB1, AXIN1, LEF1, DKK4, APCDD1) and enhanced protein-processing and translational machinery (ER processing, ribosome, rRNA/ribosome biogenesis), as well as mitochondrial gene expression and oxidative phosphorylation.  Conversely, innate-immunity and cilium-assembly programs are suppressed.  This dual pattern suggests that CTNNB1 activating mutations promote proteostasis and biosynthesis to support tumor growth while repressing differentiation-related and immune-related processes.  

Targeted (Keyword-Guided) Subset  
Filtering the full GSEA output for “Wnt” terms highlighted a single upregulated KEGG Wnt signaling pathway (hsa04310; NES = 4.28, FDR = 9.3 × 10⁻⁴) with leading genes DKK4, CTNNB1, AXIN1, LEF1, APCDD1—directly tying the differential proteomic signature to CTNNB1 mutation.  No downregulated Wnt-related terms were observed at FDR < 0.05.

Comparisons  
These patterns align with known CTNNB1 activation in endometrial tumors, where nuclear β-catenin drives Wnt target genes and biosynthetic pathways.  Suppression of ciliogenesis and complement is consistent with a pro-proliferative, immune-evasive phenotype.  No discordant single-modality findings were noted in this proteomic dataset.

Implications  
The proteomic upregulation of Wnt signaling and proteostasis machinery in CTNNB1-mutant EC suggests potential vulnerabilities to inhibitors of ER stress responses or ribosome biogenesis.  Downregulation of cilium biogenesis factors may reflect altered cell polarity that cooperates with Wnt activation to drive oncogenesis.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Functionally validate enhanced ER stress/UPR activation in CTNNB1-mutant tumors (e.g., measure BiP/HSPA5 induction).  
2. Assess dependency on ribosome biogenesis using Pol I inhibitors in patient-derived EC models.  
3. Examine the relationship between CTNNB1 S45 phosphorylation loss and Wnt target gene activation via TCF/LEF reporter assays.  
4. Investigate complement pathway suppression’s impact on immune infiltration in CTNNB1-mutant EC specimens.
